strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.16.2	self-approved ways, God weighs spirits	The commentary's worst loser thinks his own work good and cannot see his deficit; this proverb says all a person's ways look pure in his own eyes while the Lord weighs the spirits.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.21.2	self-approved way, Lord weighs hearts	The commentary combines undetected wandering with a final true balance; here every human way seems right to its owner, but the Lord weighs hearts.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.62.10	rich and poor alike light on scales	The commentary's scale finds the person, not goods, deficient and disregards rank; the psalm calls people of low and high estate alike a breath, rising together on the balance as lighter than breath.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.16.11	just scales belong to the Lord	The commentary joins the marketplace balance to God's true balance; Proverbs says honest scales and balances are the Lord's, and the weights in a merchant's bag are his work.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Mic.6.10	wicked treasures and short measure	The commentary's trader accumulates money by reducing another's measure; Micah places ill-gotten treasures beside a scant measure under divine accusation.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Mic.6.11	wicked scales and deceptive weight bag	The commentary's manipulated weights can appear balanced while cheating the buyer; Micah asks whether one can be acquitted with wicked scales and a bag of deceitful weights.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Lev.19.36	honest weights and measures as covenant duty	The commentary's two kinds of market fraud involve weighing and measuring; Leviticus commands honest balances, weights, ephah and hin together.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.25.14	large and small measures in one house	The commentary describes a seller taking full measure but giving short measure; Deuteronomy forbids keeping a large and a small measure at home, extending its adjacent ban on unequal weights to volume.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Amos.8.6	fraud enriches seller by taking the poor	The commentary says the fraudulent seller reduces another person's capital while growing his own; Amos continues the false-balance scene with merchants buying the poor for silver and selling even grain sweepings.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Prov.11.24	root table خ س ر / Hebrew חסר, sound correspondence	The commentary's loss account can reverse apparent financial gain; Proverbs says one gives freely and increases, while another withholds what is due and comes to מַחְסוֹר, want.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.13.7	appearing rich while possessing nothing	The commentary separates a cheerful or prosperous appearance from the actual account; Proverbs describes one who pretends to be rich yet has nothing, and another who seems poor yet has great wealth.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.16.8	little with righteousness better than unjust revenues	The commentary measures profit by righteous action rather than growing receipts; the proverb values a little with righteousness above large revenues gained by injustice.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.103.16	wind passes, bloom and place disappear	The commentary's storm can erase a lifetime's cultivated produce and the person who owned it; the psalm's wind passes over the mortal's flower so it is gone and its place knows it no more.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Ps.103.15	root table ء ن س / Hebrew אנש, BDB Arabic cognate	The commentary's generic insan spends a mortal lifetime as capital; this psalm calls the human אֱנוֹשׁ and compares his days to grass and his brief flourishing to a field flower.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.28.17	truthful measure sweeps false refuge away	The commentary connects a true scale with shelter from destructive weather; Isaiah makes justice a measuring line, then says hail will sweep away a refuge of lies and water flood its hiding place.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.1.3	rooted tree bears fruit and prospers in season	The commentary's alternative to losing a lifetime's crop is good work that survives its allotted time; the righteous person in the psalm is a watered tree yielding fruit in season and prospering in what he does.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.1.4	wicked driven by wind like chaff	The commentary's lost traveler and ruined crop meet the psalm's contrast: unlike the fruitful rooted tree, the wicked are chaff carried away by the wind.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Exod.13.21	fire at night guides people on their way	The commentary joins Moses' noticed fire, a night journey and hoped-for guidance; Exodus tells of the Lord leading travelers by a pillar of fire at night so they can travel.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:1Sam.16.7	human sees surface, God sees heart	The commentary says a being equipped to see can remain blind to his own real state; Samuel is told humans look at outward appearance while the Lord looks at the heart.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.12.15	fool trusts own way, wise hears advice	The commentary's mistaken confidence in one's path meets its remedy of counsel from another; the proverb says the fool's way is right in his own eyes but the wise listens to advice.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.11.14	many counselors protect against a fall	The commentary moves from one human lost alone to people helping one another find a way; the proverb says a people falls without guidance and finds safety in many counselors.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Eccl.4.9	two workers gain a better reward	The commentary joins labor and its wage to companionship as an escape from loss; Ecclesiastes says two are better than one because they have a good reward for their toil.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Eccl.4.10	companion lifts the one who falls	The commentary's lost solitary human needs another's help; Ecclesiastes blesses the one whose companion lifts him after a fall and laments the one alone with no one to lift him.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.27.6	faithful wounds from a friend	The commentary's true counsel is also likened to an accurate blow that does not miss its mark; the proverb makes even a friend's wounds faithful, giving correction a concrete and costly social form.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:2Sam.12.4	rich man takes poor man's only lamb	The commentary's dishonest seller secretly consumes another's principal; Nathan's parable has a rich man spare his own livestock and take the poor man's single cherished lamb instead.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:2Sam.12.7	another's story exposes one's hidden guilt	The commentary's seeing human needs another person's truthful address to see himself; after David condemns the parable's rich man, Nathan tells David that he is that man.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Eccl.12.14	all deeds including hidden ones judged	The commentary says loss can grow unseen until a final account reveals it; Ecclesiastes says God brings every deed and every hidden thing, good or evil, into judgment.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Dan.5.26	days of kingdom numbered and ended	The commentary treats passing time as capital spent toward an appointed reckoning; immediately before Daniel's verdict of deficient weight, he explains that God has numbered the king's days and ended his reign.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Dan.5.28	weighed king loses kingdom	The commentary says the deficient person can lose far more than goods; immediately after Daniel finds the king lacking on the balance, he declares the kingdom divided and given away.
strong	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Mishnah Avot 2:1	weigh a commandment's loss against reward	The commentary reads loss and gain as a moral account rather than an emotion; Avot tells a person to reckon the loss of a commandment against its reward and a transgression's reward against its loss.
strong	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Shabbat 31a	final judgment asks about honest business	The commentary's market fraud is answered by a later scale for the trader himself; the Talmud says that when one is brought to judgment, one is asked whether one conducted business faithfully.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.3.18	buy true gold and salve for blind eyes	The commentary joins false wealth to a seeing being who misses his own loss; the speaker follows Laodicea's unrecognized poverty by urging it to buy refined gold and eye salve so it may see.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.20.12	great and small judged from books of deeds	The commentary's verdict includes every rank and opens a ledger of deeds; Revelation has the dead, great and small, stand before a throne as books are opened and they are judged by recorded works.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.12.18	fool enlarges barns for surplus crops	The commentary says counted accumulation can mask the loss of life's principal; in the rich fool's own plan, larger barns will hold his abundant grain and goods just before his life is required.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.12.19	stored goods mistaken for years of life	The commentary's trader mistakes growing assets for safety while time is vanishing; the rich fool tells his soul that goods stored for many years let him rest, eat and drink, an error exposed by the next verse.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:James.4.14	unseen tomorrow, life as brief vapor	The commentary's expiring time is capital people cannot safely count in advance; James says they do not know tomorrow and their life appears briefly like vapor before vanishing.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.6.19	earthly treasure eaten and stolen	The commentary's apparently accumulating store is exposed to real depletion; Jesus warns that earthly treasure is destroyed by moth and rust and broken into by thieves.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.6.20	store lasting treasure elsewhere	The commentary sets profitable righteous action against perishing capital; Jesus directs hearers to store treasure in heaven, where the losses named in the preceding verse do not consume it.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Tim.6.18	rich in good deeds and generous sharing	The commentary's exception names good work while money can be lost; Paul tells the wealthy to be rich in good works and ready to share, turning abundance into action for others.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Tim.6.19	good deeds lay up future treasure and life	The commentary's true balance measures what endures beyond a lifetime; Paul says generous people store a good foundation for the future and take hold of real life.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Cor.13.3	give everything yet gain nothing without love	The commentary links good deeds to reciprocal human relations as the route out of loss; Paul says even giving away all possessions yields no gain if love is absent.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rom.2.7	enduring good work receives life	The commentary's rescue from loss joins righteous works with patience; Paul promises eternal life to those who persist in doing good while seeking glory, honor and immortality.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.10.36	endurance after doing God's will	The commentary's third verse combines good action and mutual counsel in patience; Hebrews says endurance is needed so that, after doing God's will, people receive what was promised.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.3.8	fruit as evidence of repentance	The commentary sets moral action rather than inherited status as the decisive separation from universal loss; John the Baptist calls for fruit worthy of repentance before confronting reliance on ancestry.
strong	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:Matt.3.9	Abrahamic descent no guarantee	The commentary says noble or low origin does not determine who escapes loss; John warns hearers not to presume that having Abraham as father suffices, since God can raise children for him from stones.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:John.8.39	Abraham's children shown by deeds	The commentary makes action rather than lineage the visible difference among humans; Jesus answers an appeal to Abrahamic descent by demanding the works of Abraham from those claiming to be his children.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:James.1.23	man sees his own face in a mirror	The commentary's reflected little human in another's eye is tied to truthful counsel and action; James compares a hearer who fails to act to a man looking at his own face in a mirror.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:James.1.24	forgets own face immediately after seeing	The commentary says a seeing being can miss his own deficit; James' mirror-gazer walks away and at once forgets what he looked like, making self-sight ineffective without lasting response.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:James.5.19	another turns a wanderer from truth	The commentary unites truth, a lost path and mutual counsel; James addresses believers whose companion wanders from truth and whom another person turns back.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:James.5.20	returning wanderer saves life from death	The commentary says straying can progress from depleted provisions to self-loss; James says one who brings a sinner back from wandering saves a soul from death.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Gal.6.1	gentle correction with self-watchfulness	The commentary's reciprocal counsel must repair a lost person without forgetting one's own vulnerability; Paul tells the spiritual to restore someone caught in a trespass while watching themselves.
strong	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:Luke.15.12	younger son receives his estate early	The commentary cites guardians withholding an orphan's property until maturity is discerned; in Jesus' parable the father gives the younger son his share on request, setting up a different narrative treatment of entrusted capital rather than a competing legal rule.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.15.13	son squanders entrusted property far from home	The commentary moves from handed-over capital to lost direction and finally self-loss; the younger son leaves home and dissipates his estate in reckless living before he comes to himself.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.7.25	storm cannot ruin house on rock	The commentary's shelter contrasts with exposure to destructive weather; Jesus' rain, flood and wind strike the house built on rock, but it does not fall because of its foundation.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Job.7.17	root table ء ن س / Hebrew אנש, BDB Arabic cognate	The commentary's generic insan is a vulnerable being under a sweeping verdict; Job asks what אֱנוֹשׁ is that God magnifies him and attends to him. Job's question concerns oppressive divine attention in its context, making the emotional direction different from the psalmic praise of human regard.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Job.7.18	every morning and moment tested	The commentary pictures the person's condition as continuous rather than one past loss; Job complains that God visits and tests him every morning and every moment, a darker continuous scrutiny.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Job.4.17	root table ء ن س / Hebrew אנש, BDB Arabic cognate	The commentary's universal human verdict meets Eliphaz's question whether mortal אֱנוֹשׁ can be righteous before God or pure before his maker; the connection is qualified because the claim is made within Eliphaz's disputable speech.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.49.13	high-status human perishes like a beast	The commentary refuses to separate noble from low human beings in its loss verdict and develops tame and wild animal imagery; the psalm says a human in honor cannot remain and becomes like beasts that perish.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.22.2	rich and poor share one maker	The commentary's human includes both high and low status before any exception is counted; Proverbs says rich and poor meet together because the Lord is maker of them all.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Eccl.4.12	companions resist attack like a strong cord	The commentary makes connection with others a refuge on the exposed road; Ecclesiastes says two can withstand an attacker and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.
medium	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Mishnah Avot 3:15	free choice and judgment by weight of deeds	The commentary holds a universal condition beside action that distinguishes an exception; R. Akiva's saying in Avot places human choice beside judgment according to the preponderance of deeds.
medium	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Mishnah Avot 4:1	wisdom learned from every person	The commentary turns the solitary named human toward reciprocal truth telling; Avot calls wise the person who learns from every person, making another human a source of self-correction.
medium	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Mishnah Avot 4:1	true richness as contentment with share	The commentary warns that counting more possessions can conceal actual loss; the same Avot saying calls rich the person content with his portion, redefining wealth without an expanding hoard.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Exod.3.1	Moses tends flock at Horeb	The commentary's Qur'anic account sets Moses on a journey with his family when he notices fire; Exodus introduces him tending Jethro's flock at Horeb, a specific change in the scene surrounding the same fire encounter.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.40.7	breath or wind withers the flower	The commentary's destructive wind erases growth that seemed secure; Isaiah says grass withers and flowers fade when the Lord's breath blows on them, making human flourishing fragile.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:James.1.25	persevering doer blessed in deed	The commentary's way out of loss includes action and patience after seeing truth; James contrasts the forgetful mirror-gazer with one who looks into the law, perseveres and acts, receiving blessing in the doing.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Eph.5.16	making use of the time	The commentary imagines the passing hour as capital available for good work; Ephesians urges readers to make the most of time because the days are evil.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Tim.6.9	desire for riches leads to ruin	The commentary says financial increase can carry a person toward destruction rather than profit; Paul says those determined to be rich fall into desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Mark.10.21	sell possessions for lasting treasure	The commentary's profitable trade exchanges perishable capital for righteous action; Jesus tells the wealthy man to sell what he has, give to the poor, and gain treasure in heaven.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Cor.3.14	work surviving fire receives reward	The commentary contrasts the consumed lifetime crop with enduring good work; Paul completes the fire-testing image by saying the builder whose work remains will receive a reward.
medium	incil	motif	Didache 1:1	two ways of life and death	The commentary treats loss as a misdirected path that ends in destruction and truth as another way; the Didache opens with two ways, one of life and one of death, rather than treating the error as a mere feeling.
medium	incil	motif	Gospel of Thomas 3	unrecognized poverty and self-knowledge	The commentary says the named seeing human may not perceive his own deficit; Thomas has Jesus say those who fail to know themselves dwell in poverty and are poverty, making an internal condition invisible to its bearer.
weak	incil	motif	Epistle of Barnabas 18:1	ways of light and darkness	The commentary develops losing one's way as a moral loss answered by truthful direction; Barnabas introduces opposing ways of light and darkness. The overlap is the two-path framework, since its particular signs differ from the commentary's trade and scale imagery.
EOF",max_output_tokens:1000});text(r);
